title: Faithfulness in marriage
hookLine: fidelity in marriage as part of rehat

lines: A RULE THAT LIVES AT HOME.
cards: A ring on a kitchen windowsill, set down while someone does the dishes. A kara on a wrist, never taken off at all. Two small circles, two kinds of promise.
Most of the Sikh code has looked outward: what to wear, eat and drink, how to bow. Today's rule lives somewhere quieter: at home, between two people, on ordinary days when nobody else is watching.
The code names faithfulness in marriage as part of a Sikh's rehat. Why does a code about turbans and prayers reach into a marriage?

teach.h: ADULTERY: ONE OF THE FOUR AVOIDED.

teach.b: The Rehat Maryada asks a Sikh to keep to their own spouse and to look on others with respect: in paraphrase, a man is to regard another's wife as his mother or sister, and a woman another's husband as her father or brother.
Adultery is named among the four things the initiated must never do, on the same short list as cutting the hair and using tobacco.
That placement says something: for a Sikh who has taken amrit, faithfulness is as much a part of the vow as the kesh. Second, the picture behind it.

teach.h: ANG 788: ONE LIGHT IN TWO BODIES.
teach.b: In a verse by Guru Amar Das on Ang 788, in paraphrase: they are not husband and wife who merely sit together; they are husband and wife who are one light in two bodies. A marriage isn't two people sharing a house.
It's one light living in two forms. Third, the portrait of a good life in the Sukhmani Sahib, on Ang 274, includes eyes that don't dwell on another's spouse.
Faithfulness starts small, with where the eyes rest, long before anything happens. Fourth, notice how it fits the Anand Karaj, the wedding you met earlier in this block.
The couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib together, and the hymns of that walk are about the soul's marriage to God.
Some readers hear the two marriages leaning on each other: keeping faith with a spouse as practice for keeping faith with God, and the other way around.
On that reading, the vow at home and the vow to the Guru are the same kind of promise.

how: The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs to be faithful to their spouse, and at amrit initiates are told that adultery is one of four things they must never do.

games.q: according to Guru Amar Das's verse, what makes two people husband and wife?
o: one light living in two bodies.
games.why: Ang 788: they are not husband and wife who merely sit together; they are husband and wife who are one light in two bodies.

practice: Bring to mind one promise you've made to someone you live with or love: a vow, or something small, like I'll call on Sundays, or I'll be home by six. Notice how it's going, without scolding yourself.
Then choose one small way to keep it, and let that settle into the breath.

wordCard.voice: Faithfulness in marriage. In the Sikh code, fidelity is part of rehat, and adultery is one of the four things the initiated must never do. Guru Amar Das calls a true couple one light in two bodies. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: light. Guru Amar Das calls a true couple 'one light in two bodies'.

carryVoice: Your line: faithful. One light in two bodies, kept on ordinary days. Back tomorrow, same hill.
